note: The stone bank of the stream that crosses the burning sand (Canto 14). The steam above it puts out the falling fire, so the poets can walk along it unharmed, raised above the plain.
The people of Flanders, on the North Sea coast, whose low land was kept dry by sea dikes. Dante may have seen them, or heard of them from the many Florentine merchants who traded there.

Bruges was the great trading city of Flanders. Dante's other town is Guizzante, which most scholars now take to be Wissant, a port near Calais. Others identify it with Cadzand, an island north of Bruges.
A river that comes down from the Alps and passes near Padua. When the mountain snow melts in spring it floods. Dante's Italian names the mountain region where the thaw begins, Chiarentana.
Hell is God's work, as the inscription on its gate says (Canto 3). The vague phrase may also allow for some lesser power carrying out the design.
The wood of the suicides (Canto 13), now far behind them.

The sodomites, whom Dante classes as violent against nature (Canto 11). They must keep walking over the sand under the fire, in separate bands that may not mix. The sin itself is never named in this canto.
A night with almost no moonlight, when people passing on a road peer at each other. The plain is dark except for the falling fire.

quote: like an old tailor threading a needle
note: One of Dante's best-known homely similes. It brings the workshops of an Italian town into Hell.
Dante is up on the bank and the souls are below on the sand, so the man can reach only the bottom of his gown. The teacher now walks at his pupil's feet.

A cry of surprise, and one of the poem's famous lines. "Master" translates ser, the title of a notary. Readers still argue over how to take the meeting: Dante shows the man love and respect, yet it is Dante who put him here.

context: No other record accuses him of the sin punished here. He was about forty-five years older than Dante and no schoolmaster: he was a guide and example to the young poet, and calls him "my son".

note: A rule of this ring. A soul that stops walking must lie still for a century, unable even to brush the fire off, like the blasphemers of Canto 14.
Dante can't come down onto the burning sand, so he honors his old master the only way he can, walking bent toward him.

context: Dante answers Brunetto's question without ever giving Virgil's name. Why he holds it back is not explained.

note: The dark forest of Canto 1.
Dante left the forest at dawn on Good Friday. It is now nearing dawn on Saturday: the journey through Hell so far has taken less than a day.
Home may be the right path of life, or Heaven, the soul's true home. The road there goes through Hell.

Brunetto may speak as an astrologer or just mean Dante's destiny. Dante was born under the sign of Gemini, the Twins, which was thought to favor learning and writing, and he thanks those stars for his talent in Paradiso 22.

quote: if I had not died so early
note: Brunetto died in 1294, an old man. He means too early for Dante, who was then about 29 and at the start of his public career.

context: Brunetto calls the bad Florentines the descendants of Fiesole, still as hard and rough as the mountain they came down from.

note: A prophecy of Dante's exile. In 1302, while he was away from the city, his political enemies condemned him on trumped-up charges of corruption, and then to death by burning if he ever returned. The poem is set in 1300, so what had already happened can be foretold.
The sorb is a tree with small sour fruit. Dante is the sweet fig growing in the wrong orchard.
"Blind Florentines" was an old Tuscan taunt. The chroniclers of Dante's time explained it by stories in which the city let itself be tricked.

The Black and the White Guelphs, the two factions fighting for Florence in 1300. Dante was a White. The Blacks exiled him, and he later broke with his fellow exiles too. The Italian can mean that both will hunger for him or hunger to devour him.

quote: the grass will be far from the goat
note: A proverb: they won't get their teeth into him. Dante will be out of reach of both sides.
The few Florentines who descend from the Roman founders. Brunetto counts Dante among them. For Dante, Rome was chosen by God to give the world law and peace, so Roman blood is holy.
Dead. If Dante had his wish, Brunetto would still be alive.

Through fame: by great deeds and above all by writing, a man lives on in memory. It is the only eternity Brunetto taught, and the only one he has. He still lives in his book while his soul is in Hell.
The earlier prophecy of his exile, spoken by the Ghibelline leader Farinata among the heretics (Inferno 10).

context: Virgil promised in Inferno 10 that she would explain Dante's future. In the event it is his ancestor Cacciaguida who spells out the exile, in Paradiso 17.
Dante says he is ready for whatever comes. Let Fortune turn her wheel and the peasant his hoe: each to his own work.

quote: He listens well who takes note
note: A proverb, and Virgil's only words in the canto. Usually read as approval: Dante has remembered what Virgil taught him about Fortune in Canto 7.
In Dante's day most men of learning were in holy orders. Brunetto's band is made up of churchmen and scholars. The band in Canto 16 holds soldiers and statesmen.

A Latin grammarian who taught in Constantinople about 500. His grammar was the standard textbook of the Middle Ages. Nothing is known that would explain his place here, and he may simply stand for teachers of grammar as a class.
A famous professor of law at Bologna (1225–1293), son of the great Florentine jurist Accursius. He spent some years in England in the service of King Edward I.

context: "Servant of the servants of God" is a title the popes use of themselves. In Brunetto's mouth, about this pope, it sounds sarcastic.

quote: from the Arno to the Bacchiglione
note: From Florence, on the Arno, to Vicenza, on the Bacchiglione. The man is Andrea de' Mozzi, bishop of Florence from 1287, who was moved to Vicenza in 1295 after scandal and died there soon afterward.
The Italian speaks of his "ill-strained sinews", a hint at his sexual sins. It is as close as the canto comes to naming them.
The dust and steam raised by another band coming over the sand. The groups are kept apart, and Brunetto must not be caught among souls not his own.

Li Livres dou Tresor, The Books of the Treasure, an encyclopedia of history, natural science, ethics, rhetoric and politics that Brunetto wrote in French during his exile in France in the 1260s. It was widely read for two centuries.
A foot race run each year outside Verona on the first Sunday of Lent. The runners ran naked and the winner's prize was a length of green cloth. Dante lived in Verona during his exile.

quote: not the one who loses, but the one who wins
note: One of the great closing lines of the poem. Brunetto runs naked over burning sand to catch up with the damned, and Dante's last image of him is of a winner.
